title: Cardiac output: how much the heart pumps
goal: Explain cardiac output as heart rate × stroke volume, how big it gets at rest and at maximal exercise in untrained people and elite endurance athletes, and why it sets the ceiling on VO₂max.

steps.title: Heart rate × stroke volume
steps.text:
[Cardiac output](g:cardiac-output) (Q) is the volume of blood one ventricle pumps in a minute. It is the product of two numbers [[c:cvo-q-equation]]:

**Q = HR × SV**

- **HR**, heart rate, in beats·min⁻¹;
- **SV**, [stroke volume](g:stroke-volume): the blood pushed out per beat, in mL.

Because the two circuits run in series (anatomy module), the left and right ventricles pump the same Q.

At rest, a young man's heart beats about 70 times a minute and pushes out about 70 mL each beat: about **5 L·min⁻¹** [[c:cvo-q-rest]]. That is roughly your whole blood volume, once a minute.

Watch the units: mL × beats·min⁻¹ gives mL·min⁻¹. Divide by 1000 for L·min⁻¹.

claims.text: Cardiac output is stroke volume multiplied by heart rate.

evidence.quote: To calculate this value, multiply stroke volume (SV), the amount of blood pumped by each ventricle, by heart rate (HR), in contractions per minute (or beats per minute, bpm).

claims.text: At rest, cardiac output is about 5 L·min⁻¹ in young healthy men, from about 70 beats·min⁻¹ and about 70 mL per beat.

evidence.quote: This cardiac output is achieved via a combination of a heart rate of ∼70 beats per minute (bpm) and a stroke volume of ∼70 ml/beat.

steps.title: Cardiac output at rest
steps.problem: A trained triathlete rests at 48 beats·min⁻¹ with a stroke volume of 105 mL. What is her cardiac output?
steps: Q = HR × SV = 48 beats·min⁻¹ × 105 mL = 5,040 mL·min⁻¹.
Divide by 1000: Q = 5.04 L·min⁻¹, about 5 L·min⁻¹.
The same sum turned round gives SV: SV = Q ÷ HR = 5,040 mL·min⁻¹ ÷ 48 beats·min⁻¹ = 105 mL. (Turn L·min⁻¹ back into mL·min⁻¹ first.)
She moves the same 5 L·min⁻¹ as an untrained person at 70 × 70 mL, with fewer, bigger beats.

steps.title: From 5 to 20, or to 40
steps.text:
In maximal exercise, Q climbs from about 5 to about **20 L·min⁻¹** in an untrained young man. In elite endurance athletes, values near **40 L·min⁻¹** have been reported [[c:cvo-q-max]].

| | HR (beats·min⁻¹) | SV (mL) | Q (L·min⁻¹) |
|---|---|---|---|
| rest | ~70 | ~70 | ~5 |
| max, untrained | ~200 | ~100 | ~20 |
| max, elite | similar | up to ~200 | 35–40 |

The elite heart doesn't beat much faster at max. Almost all the extra comes from a much bigger stroke volume [[c:cvo-elite-sv]]. In one study, five elite runners reached a maximal SV of 187 mL and a Q of 33.8 L·min⁻¹; untrained students reached 128 mL and 21.3 L·min⁻¹ [[c:cvo-zhou]].

claims.text: Maximal cardiac output is about 20 L·min⁻¹ in untrained young men (HR about 200 beats·min⁻¹, SV about 100 mL) and 35–40 L·min⁻¹ in elite male endurance athletes.

evidence.quote: At rest, cardiac output is ∼5 l/min and rises to ∼20 l/min in the untrained subject during maximum exercise. Values of ∼40 l/min have been reported in elite endurance athletes.
During maximum exercise, heart rate increases to values of ∼200 bpm in young healthy humans.
In reference man, a stroke volume of ∼100 ml/beat would be typical, meaning that maximum cardiac output might reach a value of ∼20 l/min.
Thus a maximum cardiac output of 35–40 l/min is possible in elite male endurance athletes.

claims.text: Elite endurance athletes' high maximal cardiac output comes almost entirely from very large stroke volumes, up to about 200 mL per beat.

evidence.quote: Almost all of this, compared with their well-trained but nonelite counterparts, is due to very large stroke volumes.
Values of ∼200 ml/beat have been reported using invasive techniques in otherwise normal-sized men

Elite endurance athletes have a high .VO(2,max) due primarily to a high cardiac output from a large compliant cardiac chamber (including the myocardium and pericardium) which relaxes quickly and fills to a large end-diastolic volume.

claims.text: Elite male distance runners reached a maximal SV of 187 mL and Q of 33.8 L·min⁻¹, against 128 mL and 21.3 L·min⁻¹ in untrained men.

evidence.quote: Moreover, the elite distance runners showed a further slope increase in SV when heart rate was above 160 bpm, which resulted in an average maximal SV of 187 +/- 14 mL x beat(-1) compared with 145 +/- 8 and 128 +/- 14 mL x beat(-1) in the university runners and untrained students, respectively (P < 0.001).
Similarly, max Q reached 33.8 +/- 2.3, 26.3 +/- 1.7, and 21.3 +/- 1.5 L x min(-1) in the three groups, respectively (P < 0.001).

steps.title: Why Q sets the ceiling on VO₂max
steps.text:
Oxygen uptake is blood flow times what each litre of blood gives up: the Fick principle you met for one muscle, now for the whole body [[c:cvo-fick-equation]]:

**VO₂ = Q × [a-vO₂ difference](g:a-vo2-difference)**

In an untrained man at max, each litre of blood gives up about 140–150 mL of O₂. So 20 L·min⁻¹ of Q supports about 3 L·min⁻¹ of VO₂ [[c:cvo-fick-reference]].

Which side limits [VO₂max](g:vo2max)? Mainly delivery [[c:cvo-delivery-limit]]. VO₂max moves when O₂ delivery changes (blood doping, low-oxygen air, β-blockers: drugs that slow the heart). And the rise in VO₂max with training comes mainly from a higher maximal Q, not a bigger a-vO₂ difference.

The oxygen transport module works through the Fick equation; the VO₂max module weighs the limits.

claims.text: VO₂max is bounded by the Fick equation: stroke volume × heart rate × arteriovenous O₂ difference.

evidence.quote: Maximal oxygen uptake (.VO(2,max)) is a physiological characteristic bounded by the parametric limits of the Fick equation: (left ventricular (LV) end-diastolic volume--LV end-systolic volume) x heart rate x arterio-venous oxygen difference.

claims.text: In an untrained man at maximal exercise, about 140–150 mL of O₂ is extracted per litre of cardiac output, giving a VO₂ of about 3 L·min⁻¹ from about 20 L·min⁻¹.

evidence.quote: This means that ∼140–150 ml of oxygen is extracted by the peripheral tissues for each liter of cardiac output.

claims.text: In whole-body exercise, VO₂max is limited mainly by O₂ delivery, and training raises it mainly through a higher maximal cardiac output.

evidence.quote: This is shown by three major lines of evidence: 1) when oxygen delivery is altered (by blood doping, hypoxia, or beta-blockade), VO2max changes accordingly; 2) the increase in VO2max with training results primarily from an increase in maximal cardiac output (not an increase in the a-v O2 difference); and 3) when a small muscle mass is overperfused during exercise, it has an extremely high capacity for consuming oxygen.
Thus, O2 delivery, not skeletal muscle O2 extraction, is viewed as the primary limiting factor for VO2max in exercising humans.

steps.title: VO₂ from cardiac output
steps.problem: At maximal effort a cyclist's Q is 25 L·min⁻¹, and each litre of blood gives up 160 mL of O₂. What is his VO₂?
steps: VO₂ = Q × a-vO₂ difference = 25 L·min⁻¹ × 160 mL·L⁻¹.
Raise Q by 10% to 27.5 L·min⁻¹ with the same extraction, and VO₂ rises 10% too: 27.5 × 160 = 4,400 mL·min⁻¹ = 4.4 L·min⁻¹.

steps.title: About 6 litres of blood per litre of oxygen
steps.text:
How does Q keep up as you go harder? Each litre of arterial blood carries about 200 mL of O₂, and the body never takes all of it. So, roughly, it takes about **6 L of cardiac output for every litre** of whole-body VO₂ [[c:cvo-six-to-one]].

That ratio explains the numbers you've seen: a VO₂ of 3 L·min⁻¹ needs about 18–20 L·min⁻¹ of Q; an elite 5.5 L·min⁻¹ needs about 33 L·min⁻¹.

Sex and size matter too. Maximal Q is about 20–40 L·min⁻¹ in healthy young men and 15–30 L·min⁻¹ in healthy young women, the top of each range being elite endurance athletes [[c:cvo-sex-range]]. Bigger bodies carry bigger hearts, which is one reason VO₂ is often compared per kg.

claims.text: With about 200 mL of O₂ per litre of arterial blood, it takes about 6 L of cardiac output for every litre of whole-body O₂ uptake.

evidence.quote: Since oxygen consumption by nonexercising tissues does not increase, and based on the idea that each liter of arterial blood carries 200 ml of oxygen, it then takes ∼6 liters of cardiac output for every liter of whole body oxygen consumption

claims.text: Maximal cardiac output ranges about 20–40 L·min⁻¹ in healthy young men and 15–30 L·min⁻¹ in healthy young women, the upper ends being elite endurance athletes.

evidence.quote: Thus, if we take the range of cardiac outputs in normal humans to be between 20 and 40 l/min for healthy young men, and 15–30 l/min for healthy young women (the upper limits in both sexes reflecting elite endurance athletes), then total muscle blood flow can reach 30–35 l/min in average-sized men who are elite endurance athletes.

steps.title: How much more blood for more oxygen?
steps.problem: A runner's VO₂ rises from 1.5 to 3.0 L·min⁻¹ as she speeds up. Using about 6 L of Q per litre of VO₂, how much does her cardiac output rise?
steps: It is a rule of thumb: the real ratio shifts with haemoglobin and with how much O₂ the muscles extract.

points: Cardiac output Q = HR × SV: about 70 beats·min⁻¹ × 70 mL ≈ 5 L·min⁻¹ at rest.
At max, Q reaches about 20 L·min⁻¹ in untrained young men and 35–40 L·min⁻¹ in elite male endurance athletes (women about 15–30).
Maximal HR is similar in trained and untrained people: the elite advantage is a much bigger stroke volume.
VO₂ = Q × a-vO₂ difference. In whole-body exercise O₂ delivery, mainly maximal Q, is the main limit on VO₂max, and training raises VO₂max mainly through Q.
Roughly 6 L of Q are needed for every litre of VO₂.

variants.stem: A cyclist rides at 150 beats·min⁻¹ with a stroke volume of 120 mL. What is his cardiac output?

options.why: Right: 150 × 120 mL = 18,000 mL·min⁻¹ = 18.0 L·min⁻¹.
This divides HR by SV (150 ÷ 120). Q is HR multiplied by SV.
The number is in mL·min⁻¹: divide by 1000 to get L·min⁻¹.
This adds HR and SV (150 + 120). They multiply.

variants.solution: Q = HR × SV = 150 beats·min⁻¹ × 120 mL = 18,000 mL·min⁻¹ = 18.0 L·min⁻¹.

variants.stem: A runner at the end of a 5 km race is at 180 beats·min⁻¹ with a stroke volume of 160 mL. What is her cardiac output?

options.why: Right: 180 × 160 mL = 28,800 mL·min⁻¹ = 28.8 L·min⁻¹.
This divides HR by SV (180 ÷ 160). Q is HR multiplied by SV.
The number is in mL·min⁻¹: divide by 1000 to get L·min⁻¹.
This adds HR and SV (180 + 160). They multiply.

variants.solution: Q = HR × SV = 180 beats·min⁻¹ × 160 mL = 28,800 mL·min⁻¹ = 28.8 L·min⁻¹.

variants.stem: A triathlete rests at 45 beats·min⁻¹ with a stroke volume of 110 mL. What is his cardiac output?

options.why: Right: 45 × 110 mL = 4,950 mL·min⁻¹ = 4.95 L·min⁻¹, a normal resting value.
This divides HR by SV (45 ÷ 110). Q is HR multiplied by SV.
The number is in mL·min⁻¹: divide by 1000 to get L·min⁻¹.
This adds HR and SV (45 + 110). They multiply.

variants.solution: Q = HR × SV = 45 beats·min⁻¹ × 110 mL = 4,950 mL·min⁻¹ = 4.95 L·min⁻¹.

variants.stem: At maximal effort, a runner's cardiac output is 30 L·min⁻¹ at 185 beats·min⁻¹. What is her stroke volume?

options.why: Right: 30,000 mL·min⁻¹ ÷ 185 beats·min⁻¹ = 162 mL.
This divides 30 by 185 without first turning L into mL (30 L = 30,000 mL).
This divides HR by Q (185 ÷ 30). SV = Q ÷ HR.
This multiplies Q by HR. SV = Q ÷ HR.

variants.solution: SV = Q ÷ HR = 30,000 mL·min⁻¹ ÷ 185 beats·min⁻¹ = 162 mL.

variants.stem: At maximal effort, a cyclist's cardiac output is 22 L·min⁻¹ at 195 beats·min⁻¹. What is his stroke volume?

options.why: Right: 22,000 mL·min⁻¹ ÷ 195 beats·min⁻¹ = 113 mL.
This divides 22 by 195 without first turning L into mL (22 L = 22,000 mL).
This divides HR by Q (195 ÷ 22). SV = Q ÷ HR.
This multiplies Q by HR. SV = Q ÷ HR.

variants.solution: SV = Q ÷ HR = 22,000 mL·min⁻¹ ÷ 195 beats·min⁻¹ = 112.8 ≈ 113 mL.

variants.stem: A healthy, untrained young man goes all out on a bike test. About how high does his cardiac output get?

options.why: Right: from about 5 L·min⁻¹ at rest to about 20 L·min⁻¹, roughly fourfold.
Only twice the resting value; Q rises about fourfold in an untrained man.
That is the top of the range, reported only in elite endurance athletes.
No human heart has been measured pumping that much.

variants.stem: An elite male endurance runner goes all out on a treadmill test. About how high can his cardiac output get?

options.why: Right: 35–40 L·min⁻¹ is possible in elite male endurance athletes.
That is the untrained value; the elite heart pumps far more.
That is only twice rest, lower than any untrained person at max.
No human heart has been measured pumping that much.

variants.stem: Two cyclists both top out at 190 beats·min⁻¹ in a ramp test. One reaches a cardiac output of 36 L·min⁻¹, the other 22 L·min⁻¹. What explains the gap?

options.why: Right: same HR, so SV must differ: 36,000 ÷ 190 ≈ 189 mL against 22,000 ÷ 190 ≈ 116 mL.
Both reach 190 beats·min⁻¹. Fitter hearts don't beat faster at max: they beat bigger.
That raises VO₂, not Q. Q depends only on HR and SV.
Thicker blood raises resistance to flow; it doesn't make the heart pump more.

variants.stem: At maximal effort, an untrained runner's cardiac output is 20 L·min⁻¹ and each litre of blood gives up 150 mL of O₂. What is his VO₂?

options.why: Right: 20 L·min⁻¹ × 150 mL·L⁻¹ = 3,000 mL·min⁻¹ = 3.0 L·min⁻¹.
This divides Q by the a-vO₂ difference (20 ÷ 150). They multiply.
The product is in mL·min⁻¹: divide by 1000 to get L·min⁻¹.
This divides the a-vO₂ difference by Q (150 ÷ 20). They multiply.

variants.solution: VO₂ = Q × a-vO₂ difference = 20 L·min⁻¹ × 150 mL·L⁻¹ = 3,000 mL·min⁻¹ = 3.0 L·min⁻¹.

variants.stem: At maximal effort, an elite cyclist's cardiac output is 35 L·min⁻¹ and each litre of blood gives up 160 mL of O₂. What is his VO₂?

options.why: Right: 35 L·min⁻¹ × 160 mL·L⁻¹ = 5,600 mL·min⁻¹ = 5.6 L·min⁻¹.
This divides Q by the a-vO₂ difference (35 ÷ 160). They multiply.
The product is in mL·min⁻¹: divide by 1000 to get L·min⁻¹.
This divides the a-vO₂ difference by Q (160 ÷ 35). They multiply.

variants.solution: VO₂ = Q × a-vO₂ difference = 35 L·min⁻¹ × 160 mL·L⁻¹ = 5,600 mL·min⁻¹ = 5.6 L·min⁻¹.

variants.stem: At maximal effort, a triathlete's cardiac output is 28 L·min⁻¹ and each litre of blood gives up 155 mL of O₂. What is her VO₂?

options.why: Right: 28 L·min⁻¹ × 155 mL·L⁻¹ = 4,340 mL·min⁻¹ = 4.34 L·min⁻¹.
This divides Q by the a-vO₂ difference (28 ÷ 155). They multiply.
The product is in mL·min⁻¹: divide by 1000 to get L·min⁻¹.
This divides the a-vO₂ difference by Q (155 ÷ 28). They multiply.

variants.solution: VO₂ = Q × a-vO₂ difference = 28 L·min⁻¹ × 155 mL·L⁻¹ = 4,340 mL·min⁻¹ = 4.34 L·min⁻¹.

variants.stem: Which finding is the strongest sign that O₂ delivery, rather than the muscles' ability to use O₂, limits VO₂max in running or cycling?

options.text: VO₂max rises after blood doping and falls in low-oxygen air
options.why: Right: changing delivery alone moves VO₂max, one of the three main lines of evidence for a delivery limit.

options.text: Muscle mitochondrial enzymes rise a lot with training
options.why: That is a muscle adaptation. It mainly improves submaximal endurance, and on its own says nothing about delivery.

options.text: Blood lactate climbs steeply in the last minutes of a ramp
options.why: Lactate reflects glycolysis and clearance, not which step of O₂ transport is limiting.

options.text: Venous blood leaving the legs still holds some O₂ at max
options.why: Leftover O₂ fits a delivery limit but doesn't prove one; the experiments that change delivery are the strong evidence.

variants.stem: After a year of structured training, a runner's VO₂max is 15% higher. Her maximal HR is unchanged and her a-vO₂ difference at max barely moved. What most likely went up?

options.why: Right: VO₂ = HR × SV × a-vO₂ difference. With HRmax and extraction unchanged, maximal SV, and so Q, must have risen: the main route of training gains.
The stem says it is unchanged, and HRmax barely moves with training.
That is the a-vO₂ difference, which the stem says barely moved.
Resting HR usually falls with training, but it doesn't enter VO₂max at all.

variants.stem: On the bike leg, a triathlete's VO₂ rises from 2.0 to 4.0 L·min⁻¹. Using about 6 L of cardiac output per litre of VO₂, by how much does her Q rise?

options.why: This assumes 1 L of blood per litre of O₂. Each litre of blood carries only about 200 mL of O₂.
This divides the VO₂ rise by 6. Q rises by 6 times the VO₂ rise.
This multiplies the final VO₂ (4.0) by 6, not the rise (2.0).

variants.solution: Rise in VO₂ = 4.0 − 2.0 = 2.0 L·min⁻¹. Rise in Q ≈ 6 × 2.0 = 12 L·min⁻¹.

variants.stem: A runner's VO₂ rises from 1.0 to 3.5 L·min⁻¹ between a jog and a hard tempo. Using about 6 L of cardiac output per litre of VO₂, by how much does his Q rise?

options.why: This assumes 1 L of blood per litre of O₂. Each litre of blood carries only about 200 mL of O₂.
This divides the VO₂ rise by 6. Q rises by 6 times the VO₂ rise.
This multiplies the final VO₂ (3.5) by 6, not the rise (2.5).

variants.solution: Rise in VO₂ = 3.5 − 1.0 = 2.5 L·min⁻¹. Rise in Q ≈ 6 × 2.5 = 15 L·min⁻¹.
